review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta)
review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that the patch series does not change behavior on any system without private nodes, and suggested reviewing patches 1-26 separately from the rest of the series
review_comments.raw_body:
This is v6 of the Private NUMA node series. The series falls into four
parts, each building on the one before:

   1-18  mm: introduce N_MEMORY_COMMON
  19-26  restrict folio-walking MM services to common memory
  27-44  N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, kept out of cpusets, mempolicy, accounting
         and the page allocator's ordinary paths
  45-61  private node features, memory hotplug of private memory,
         dax/kmem private mode, selftests and documentation

Patches 1-26 change no behavior on any system and can be reviewed and
merged on their own. Without private nodes, every path in patches 27-61
behaves as before.

The full stack is also available at:
https://github.com/gourryinverse/linux/tree/scratch/gourry/managed_nodes/private_nodes_v6

Motivation
==========

Some memory should be visible as a NUMA node without becoming part of
the general allocation pool: HBM, coherent GPU or accelerator memory,
or device memory a driver hands out itself.

Today such memory is either ordinary System RAM, where any allocation
can fall back onto it and every MM service manages it, or ZONE_DEVICE,
where the buddy allocator and the MM services are not available at all.

Private nodes sit in between. Their memory is managed by the buddy
allocator, but ordinary allocations never land on it, and generic MM
services leave it alone unless the node opts back in.

Model
=====

  N_MEMORY = N_MEMORY_COMMON + N_MEMORY_PRIVATE

  - N_MEMORY keeps meaning "this node has memory".
  - N_MEMORY_COMMON means ordinary allocations and kernel services
    may use it.
  - Allocation isolation comes from the zonelists: a private node is
    on no fallback zonelist and has an empty __GFP_THISNODE zonelist.
    It is reached only through its own private zonelist.
  - Services that walk existing folios check folio_is_common_memory()
    where they already skip ZONE_DEVICE.
  - A private node can opt into compaction, reclaim and userspace
    placement through per-node features. The services are written in
    terms of their own node state (N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, ...), so services
    don't need to be "aware" of anything but themselves.

The node state use / filtering model goes as such:
  1) If you're walking the normal zonelists, you're already filtered
  2) If you're walking nodelists to touch memory, filter on
     N_MEMORY_COMMON by default (replacing N_MEMORY).
  3) If you're walking structures to operate on folios / pages,
     check folio_is_common_memory() (replacing zone_device checks)
  4) If the service allows private memory interactions, use the
     N_MEMORY_<FEATURE> bit corresponding to the service.

     e.g.: reclaim checks N_MEMORY_FEATURE when walking N_MEMORY
     or when walking the private memory zonelist.

N_MEMORY_COMMON (patches 1-18)
==============================

N_MEMORY has two meanings today:
  1) this node has memory
  2) ordinary allocations and MM services can use this node's memory

The two are the same today. They stop being the same once a NUMA node
with memory isn't part of the general allocation pool.

N_MEMORY_COMMON takes the second meaning, and the N_MEMORY users that
mean it are converted. N_MEMORY continues reporting memory topology.

The rule for choosing between them:

  N_MEMORY         the node has memory: topology, per-node metadata and
                   statistics, cpuset.mems.
  N_MEMORY_COMMON  ordinary allocations or a kernel service may use the
                   node's memory: zonelists, allocation and migration
                   targets, per-node service threads, and sizing or
                   accounting meant for ordinary allocations.

Code that walks the existing zonelist needs no check. The zonelists
are built from N_MEMORY_COMMON, so they already hold only memory the
allocation may use.

Unless a system actually has a private node, N_MEMORY and
N_MEMORY_COMMON are the same set, so behavior should be unchanged.

  1-3   node-state helpers, N_MEMORY_COMMON itself, and the
        `has_common_memory` sysfs ABI.
  4     zonelists: the fallback lists hold common nodes, and a node's
        __GFP_THISNODE list is built only for a common node
  5-11  allocation and migration targets
  12-13 kswapd and kcompactd
  14-18 sizing and accounting meant for ordinary allocations

has_common_memory lists the same nodes as has_memory until memory
outside N_MEMORY_COMMON exists. It is added now so that userspace, such
as libnuma, can start choosing allocation targets from it, and so that
the meaning is fixed before anything makes the two lists differ.

Folio-walking MM services (patches 19-26)
=========================================

Patches 1-18 decide where memory comes from: zonelists, allocation
targets and per-node services follow N_MEMORY_COMMON. Some MM services
instead reach folios that already exist, wherever they are: through
page tables (KSM, khugepaged, NUMA hinting, madvise, mbind() and
migrate_pages(), move_pages()) or through physical addresses (DAMON).

These services skip ZONE_DEVICE folios with folio_is_zone_device() and
page_is_zone_device().

Patch 19 generalizes those checks into folio_is_common_memory() and
page_is_common_memory(), which reject ZONE_DEVICE folios and folios
on a node outside N_MEMORY_COMMON.

The rule: a service that walks folios checks folio_is_common_memory()
where it would otherwise check folio_is_zone_device().

Rather than add new hooks to page-table and pfn walkers, this reuses the
places that already opt ZONE_DEVICE memory out.

  19    folio_is_common_memory() and page_is_common_memory()
  20-26 ZONE_DEVICE checks in folio-walking services become
        page/folio_is_common_memory(). One component per patch.

N_MEMORY_PRIVATE (patches 27-44)
================================

Patches 27-44 add the memory that makes N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_COMMON
differ. A private node has online System RAM that ordinary allocations
do not use and MM services leave alone, so neither an allocation that
names no node nor a node-local kernel allocation can land on it.

Most of these patches add the explicit opt-outs that the N_MEMORY ->
N_MEMORY_COMMON conversion did not cover, largely concentrated in
cpuset, mempolicy and migration.

In the page allocator, each node gets a private zonelist holding its
own zones only if it is private. MM code reaches private memory only
through that zonelist (ALLOC_ZONELIST_PRIVATE plus a nodemask).

A private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes onto common
memory, and exhausting private memory fails the allocation (SIGBUS on
fault) instead of invoking the OOM killer (this can change in the
future with additional work).

Nothing in patches 27-44 creates private memory. Memory hotplug of
private memory, with dax/kmem as its first user, comes in patches
56-57, after the feature bits that let a private node opt into
reclaim, compaction and userspace placement.

  27-28 N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, exported as has_private_memory.
        A per-node feature mask on the pgdat.
  29-30 accounting: MemTotal/MemFree/other limits ignore private mem.
        the auto-movable online policy ignores private memory
  31-35 cpusets and mempolicy: private nodes are inherited only on
        request, never rebound onto, never spread over, and never
        migrate_pages() destinations
  36    explicit reclaim and compaction requests refuse private nodes
  37-44 page allocator:
        37-38 the reserves and watermarks, and contiguous allocation,
              skip/refuse private memory
        39-40 the private zonelist and its selection by MM callers
        41    a private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes
              onto common memory to ensure forward progress
        42    exhausting private memory fails with SIGBUS, like an
              exhausted HugeTLB pool
        43    an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator (Brendan Jackman)
        44    a bind policy whose nodes became private falls back to
              common memory

Private node features and providers (patches 45-61)
===================================================

Patches 1-44 keep every generic MM service off private memory.

Some private memory wants a few of them back: HBM or coherent GPU
memory that userspace manages with mbind() and migrate_pages() needs
reclaim and compaction, while staying out of incidental allocation
(no fallback onto it, only explicit placement).

Patches 45-55 add three opt-in feature bits and corresponding node
states:

  N_MEMORY_COMPACTION   kcompactd, proactive and explicit compaction
  N_MEMORY_RECLAIM      kswapd, memcg and explicit reclaim
  N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY    mbind() and explicit migration may target it

The states cover what the kernel does on its own initiative. Direct
reclaim and compaction serve an allocation within its own zonelist, so
an allocation from a private node may reclaim and compact it either way.

RECLAIM requires COMPACTION, and MEMPOLICY requires both. Userspace
control (mbind, migration) generates fragmentation, and as a result
private allocations would fail unpredictably without reclaim/compaction.

Relcaim and compaction are required by mempolicy because otherwise
order-N allocations cause unpredictable out of memory conditions due
to fragmentation.

Demotion and NUMA balancing support are deferred to a later series
but can be trivially support to allow demotions from HBM to DRAM
as a way of cheap tiering.

Every common node carries all three, so the existing N_MEMORY_COMMON
users that mean "reclaim" or "compaction" move to the new states.

Service support:

  45-46 N_MEMORY_COMPACTION, and compaction switched to it
  47-48 N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, and reclaim switched to it
  49    madvise reclaim advice only for reclaim-capable memory
  50    memcg reclaim also visits private nodes that permit reclaim
  51    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY
  52    explicit migration acts on N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory
  53    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory counts as general-purpose.
        MemAvailable (free and file pages) and dirty limits count
	only common memory.
  54    MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES: mbind() flag that binds a mapping to
        one private node.
  55    migrate_pages() support for N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY nodes

Creating a private node

  56    memory hotplug of private memory, with a feature mask
  57    dax/kmem private mode

Testing and Documentation:

  58-60 selftests: private kmem devices and services, memory policy
        bindings, migration and exhaustion, and cpuset interaction
  61    Documentation/mm/numa_private_nodes.rst

MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES is new uapi. Without it, private nodes in an
mbind() mask are ignored, similar to nodes outside the cpuset.

libnuma and numactl need a matching change to reach private nodes.

There is no sysfs list of the nodes that accept private bindings.
userspace can probe with MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES.  Otherwise - we can
discuss how service support should be discoverable to userspace.

Memory hotplug is the only source of private memory right now.

All System RAM on a node shares one configuration: hotplug with a
different one fails with -EBUSY.

Costs and known limits
======================

  - ZONELIST_PRIVATE is a third zonelist per pgdat; with NODES_SHIFT=10
    that is about 80KB per possible node, though a private zonelist
    holds at most one node's zones.

    local-only zonelists can be space-optimized if this matters.

  - Free page reporting reports free private pages like any others.

  - Tasks are OOM-scored by all of their resident memory,
    private pages included.

Changes since v5 ("Private Memory NUMA Nodes")
==============================================

  - Reordered so the N_MEMORY audit (patches 1-26) comes first and can
    be reviewed (and merged) on its own if desired.
  - Capabilities became memory features with node states, so a service
    can be written in terms of itself: reclaim walks N_MEMORY_RECLAIM,
    compaction N_MEMORY_COMPACTION.
  - The capability set is pared down to COMPACTION, RECLAIM and
    MEMPOLICY for the first run.  DEMOTION, NUMA_BALANCING, and
    compressed RAM support are deferred.
  - The private zonelist is now local-only. A fallback variant can be
    added if a use case needs one.
  - cpuset and OOM semantics are worked out:
      - cpuset.mems governs private nodes
      - private-only request inherits the parent's common nodes.
  - Private bindings are an explicit uapi flag, MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES,
    rather than inferred from the nodemask.
  - Exhausting private placement fails the fault with SIGBUS, as an

Add for_each_node_mask_state(), which iterates a nodemask intersected

temporary nodemask.

do_migrate_range() / alloc_migration_target() is only capable of
allocating memory on N_MEMORY_COMMON nodes. The destination nodemask
presently starts with N_MEMORY and removes the source-node.

In the current code, if the destination mask becomes empty, the source
node is restored to allow migration during partial offlining.

Consider this configuration:
  Node0 = N_MEMORY_COMMON
  Node1 = N_MEMORY, not N_MEMORY_COMMON

Node 1 keeps the destination mask non-empty, despite being unreachable.
This leaves migration with no usable destination because the source
node is not an eligible allocation target.

Restrict the hot-unplug migration target-list to N_MEMORY_COMMON so it
reflects the nodes the allocator can reach.

Memory outside N_MEMORY_COMMON is outside the ordinary allocation pool
and cannot be a generic demotion source or destination.

Build demotion paths and the default DRAM performance reference from
N_MEMORY_COMMON rather than every node that has memory, and do not
assign other nodes to a memory tier through the generic hotplug path.

Removing a node's memory already resets its demotion targets, so a node
that unplugs and returns outside N_MEMORY_COMMON keeps none.

 }

memory policies, the destination should be general purpose memory.

... snip ...

Patch count is not what we want to be optimizing for here.

Your branch carries the same code (+3 lines net actually).

The patch reduction comes from squashing the per-subsystem conversions
into one 16-file commit.

It also broke get_mempolicy(MPOL_F_MEMS_ALLOWED) - it now returns
memoryless nodes even if the system doesn't have a private node.

> The more important thing is that N_MEMORY and the proposed N_MEMORY_NOALLOC
> is a disjoint, contrary to N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_COMMON.

The proposal here is not novel - version 5 was also disjoint:
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260720193431.3841992-5-gourry@gourry.net/

   N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_PRIVATE are mutually exclusive states.

I moved away from that because it changes the definition of N_MEMORY.

The subset model is easy to understand

N_MEMORY               - a node has memory
 -> N_HIGH_MEMORY      - subset of N_MEMORY
 -> N_NORMAL_MEMORY    - subset of N_MEMORY
 -> N_MEMORY_COMMON    - subset of N_MEMORY
 -> N_MEMORY_PRIVATE   - subset of N_MEMORY
                         (COMMON and PRIVATE partition N_MEMORY)
 -> N_MEMORY_<FEATURE> - subset of N_MEMORY
                         all N_MEMORY_COMMON
			 some N_MEMORY_PRIVATE

It's additive. Users pick the set of nodes they want for their purpose
and don't have to cobble sets together or remember special helpers.
Users don't even need to know about private nodes most of the time
(mempolicy being the one major exception here).

In the disjoint model, N_MEMORY no longer means "has memory". Recovering
that set requires new helpers, and the meaning changes silently for
every in-tree and out-of-tree user. Anything that wanted "has memory"
quietly misses private nodes.

Either way you have to audit each N_MEMORY reference and decide whether
it wants that state or a feature variant (N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, COMPACTION).

The difference is how a missed site fails. In the joint model the
zonelist and the common-memory folio checks backstop allocation and
access, so a missed placement site costs some additional work.

In the disjoint model a missed site silently drops a node from stats
and accounting - or worse fails to allocate per-node meta data.

So no, I do not think we should go back to the disjoint model.

> > And N_MEMORY_NOALLOC is not a good name.
> 
> Sure, I'm not attached to any particular name. Although,
> N_MEMORY_COMMON nothing better to me. It answers the question
> 'what for this thing' even worse.
> 

happy to wordsmith the names here.

N_MEMORY_GENERAL? _DEFAULT?  _COMMON felt intuitive but I am happy
to rename it whatever.

-- 
~Gregory

review_comments.author: Yury Norov
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Yury Norov noted that N_MEMORY has two meanings today: whether a node has memory and whether ordinary allocations can use its memory, but once private nodes are introduced, these meanings diverge. He suggested keeping N_MEMORY meaning unchanged and adding another type, like N_MEMORY_NOALLOC.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 20, 2026 at 01:08:51PM -0500, Gregory Price via B4 Relay wrote:
> This is v6 of the Private NUMA node series. The series falls into four
> parts, each building on the one before:
> 
>    1-18  mm: introduce N_MEMORY_COMMON

I walked through this part, mostly. It looks like you can substantially
decrease the patch count if you keep N_MEMORY meaning unchanged, and
add another type, like N_MEMORY_NOALLOC.

>   19-26  restrict folio-walking MM services to common memory
>   27-44  N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, kept out of cpusets, mempolicy, accounting
>          and the page allocator's ordinary paths
>   45-61  private node features, memory hotplug of private memory,
>          dax/kmem private mode, selftests and documentation
> 
> Patches 1-26 change no behavior on any system and can be reviewed and
> merged on their own. Without private nodes, every path in patches 27-61
> behaves as before.
> 
> The full stack is also available at:
> https://github.com/gourryinverse/linux/tree/scratch/gourry/managed_nodes/private_nodes_v6
> 
> Motivation
> ==========
> 
> Some memory should be visible as a NUMA node without becoming part of
> the general allocation pool: HBM, coherent GPU or accelerator memory,
> or device memory a driver hands out itself.
> 
> Today such memory is either ordinary System RAM, where any allocation
> can fall back onto it and every MM service manages it, or ZONE_DEVICE,
> where the buddy allocator and the MM services are not available at all.
> 
> Private nodes sit in between. Their memory is managed by the buddy
> allocator, but ordinary allocations never land on it, and generic MM
> services leave it alone unless the node opts back in.
> 
> Model
> =====
> 
>   N_MEMORY = N_MEMORY_COMMON + N_MEMORY_PRIVATE
> 
>   - N_MEMORY keeps meaning "this node has memory".
>   - N_MEMORY_COMMON means ordinary allocations and kernel services
>     may use it.
>   - Allocation isolation comes from the zonelists: a private node is
>     on no fallback zonelist and has an empty __GFP_THISNODE zonelist.
>     It is reached only through its own private zonelist.
>   - Services that walk existing folios check folio_is_common_memory()
>     where they already skip ZONE_DEVICE.
>   - A private node can opt into compaction, reclaim and userspace
>     placement through per-node features. The services are written in
>     terms of their own node state (N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, ...), so services
>     don't need to be "aware" of anything but themselves.
> 
> The node state use / filtering model goes as such:
>   1) If you're walking the normal zonelists, you're already filtered
>   2) If you're walking nodelists to touch memory, filter on
>      N_MEMORY_COMMON by default (replacing N_MEMORY).
>   3) If you're walking structures to operate on folios / pages,
>      check folio_is_common_memory() (replacing zone_device checks)
>   4) If the service allows private memory interactions, use the
>      N_MEMORY_<FEATURE> bit corresponding to the service.
> 
>      e.g.: reclaim checks N_MEMORY_FEATURE when walking N_MEMORY
>      or when walking the private memory zonelist.
> 
> N_MEMORY_COMMON (patches 1-18)
> ==============================
> 
> N_MEMORY has two meanings today:
>   1) this node has memory
>   2) ordinary allocations and MM services can use this node's memory
> 
> The two are the same today. They stop being the same once a NUMA node
> with memory isn't part of the general allocation pool.
> 
> N_MEMORY_COMMON takes the second meaning, and the N_MEMORY users that
> mean it are converted. N_MEMORY continues reporting memory topology.
> 
> The rule for choosing between them:
> 
>   N_MEMORY         the node has memory: topology, per-node metadata and
>                    statistics, cpuset.mems.
>   N_MEMORY_COMMON  ordinary allocations or a kernel service may use the
>                    node's memory: zonelists, allocation and migration
>                    targets, per-node service threads, and sizing or
>                    accounting meant for ordinary allocations.
> 
> Code that walks the existing zonelist needs no check. The zonelists
> are built from N_MEMORY_COMMON, so they already hold only memory the
> allocation may use.
> 
> Unless a system actually has a private node, N_MEMORY and
> N_MEMORY_COMMON are the same set, so behavior should be unchanged.
> 
>   1-3   node-state helpers, N_MEMORY_COMMON itself, and the
>         `has_common_memory` sysfs ABI.
>   4     zonelists: the fallback lists hold common nodes, and a node's
>         __GFP_THISNODE list is built only for a common node
>   5-11  allocation and migration targets
>   12-13 kswapd and kcompactd
>   14-18 sizing and accounting meant for ordinary allocations
> 
> has_common_memory lists the same nodes as has_memory until memory
> outside N_MEMORY_COMMON exists. It is added now so that userspace, such
> as libnuma, can start choosing allocation targets from it, and so that
> the meaning is fixed before anything makes the two lists differ.
> 
> Folio-walking MM services (patches 19-26)
> =========================================
> 
> Patches 1-18 decide where memory comes from: zonelists, allocation
> targets and per-node services follow N_MEMORY_COMMON. Some MM services
> instead reach folios that already exist, wherever they are: through
> page tables (KSM, khugepaged, NUMA hinting, madvise, mbind() and
> migrate_pages(), move_pages()) or through physical addresses (DAMON).
> 
> These services skip ZONE_DEVICE folios with folio_is_zone_device() and
> page_is_zone_device().
> 
> Patch 19 generalizes those checks into folio_is_common_memory() and
> page_is_common_memory(), which reject ZONE_DEVICE folios and folios
> on a node outside N_MEMORY_COMMON.
> 
> The rule: a service that walks folios checks folio_is_common_memory()
> where it would otherwise check folio_is_zone_device().
> 
> Rather than add new hooks to page-table and pfn walkers, this reuses the
> places that already opt ZONE_DEVICE memory out.
> 
>   19    folio_is_common_memory() and page_is_common_memory()
>   20-26 ZONE_DEVICE checks in folio-walking services become
>         page/folio_is_common_memory(). One component per patch.
> 
> N_MEMORY_PRIVATE (patches 27-44)
> ================================
> 
> Patches 27-44 add the memory that makes N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_COMMON
> differ. A private node has online System RAM that ordinary allocations
> do not use and MM services leave alone, so neither an allocation that
> names no node nor a node-local kernel allocation can land on it.
> 
> Most of these patches add the explicit opt-outs that the N_MEMORY ->
> N_MEMORY_COMMON conversion did not cover, largely concentrated in
> cpuset, mempolicy and migration.
> 
> In the page allocator, each node gets a private zonelist holding its
> own zones only if it is private. MM code reaches private memory only
> through that zonelist (ALLOC_ZONELIST_PRIVATE plus a nodemask).
> 
> A private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes onto common
> memory, and exhausting private memory fails the allocation (SIGBUS on
> fault) instead of invoking the OOM killer (this can change in the
> future with additional work).
> 
> Nothing in patches 27-44 creates private memory. Memory hotplug of
> private memory, with dax/kmem as its first user, comes in patches
> 56-57, after the feature bits that let a private node opt into
> reclaim, compaction and userspace placement.
> 
>   27-28 N_MEMORY_PRIVATE, exported as has_private_memory.
>         A per-node feature mask on the pgdat.
>   29-30 accounting: MemTotal/MemFree/other limits ignore private mem.
>         the auto-movable online policy ignores private memory
>   31-35 cpusets and mempolicy: private nodes are inherited only on
>         request, never rebound onto, never spread over, and never
>         migrate_pages() destinations
>   36    explicit reclaim and compaction requests refuse private nodes
>   37-44 page allocator:
>         37-38 the reserves and watermarks, and contiguous allocation,
>               skip/refuse private memory
>         39-40 the private zonelist and its selection by MM callers
>         41    a private request whose node becomes ineligible relaxes
>               onto common memory to ensure forward progress
>         42    exhausting private memory fails with SIGBUS, like an
>               exhausted HugeTLB pool
>         43    an alloc_flags-aware folio allocator (Brendan Jackman)
>         44    a bind policy whose nodes became private falls back to
>               common memory
> 
> Private node features and providers (patches 45-61)
> ===================================================
> 
> Patches 1-44 keep every generic MM service off private memory.
> 
> Some private memory wants a few of them back: HBM or coherent GPU
> memory that userspace manages with mbind() and migrate_pages() needs
> reclaim and compaction, while staying out of incidental allocation
> (no fallback onto it, only explicit placement).
> 
> Patches 45-55 add three opt-in feature bits and corresponding node
> states:
> 
>   N_MEMORY_COMPACTION   kcompactd, proactive and explicit compaction
>   N_MEMORY_RECLAIM      kswapd, memcg and explicit reclaim
>   N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY    mbind() and explicit migration may target it
> 
> The states cover what the kernel does on its own initiative. Direct
> reclaim and compaction serve an allocation within its own zonelist, so
> an allocation from a private node may reclaim and compact it either way.
> 
> RECLAIM requires COMPACTION, and MEMPOLICY requires both. Userspace
> control (mbind, migration) generates fragmentation, and as a result
> private allocations would fail unpredictably without reclaim/compaction.
> 
> Relcaim and compaction are required by mempolicy because otherwise
> order-N allocations cause unpredictable out of memory conditions due
> to fragmentation.
> 
> Demotion and NUMA balancing support are deferred to a later series
> but can be trivially support to allow demotions from HBM to DRAM
> as a way of cheap tiering.
> 
> Every common node carries all three, so the existing N_MEMORY_COMMON
> users that mean "reclaim" or "compaction" move to the new states.
> 
> Service support:
> 
>   45-46 N_MEMORY_COMPACTION, and compaction switched to it
>   47-48 N_MEMORY_RECLAIM, and reclaim switched to it
>   49    madvise reclaim advice only for reclaim-capable memory
>   50    memcg reclaim also visits private nodes that permit reclaim
>   51    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY
>   52    explicit migration acts on N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory
>   53    N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY memory counts as general-purpose.
>         MemAvailable (free and file pages) and dirty limits count
> 	only common memory.
>   54    MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES: mbind() flag that binds a mapping to
>         one private node.
>   55    migrate_pages() support for N_MEMORY_MEMPOLICY nodes
> 
> Creating a private node
> 
>   56    memory hotplug of private memory, with a feature mask
>   57    dax/kmem private mode
> 
> Testing and Documentation:
> 
>   58-60 selftests: private kmem devices and services, memory policy
>         bindings, migration and exhaustion, and cpuset interaction
>   61    Documentation/mm/numa_private_nodes.rst
> 
> MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES is new uapi. Without it, private nodes in an
> mbind() mask are ignored, similar to nodes outside the cpuset.
> 
> libnuma and numactl need a matching change to reach private nodes.
> 
> There is no sysfs list of the nodes that accept private bindings.
> userspace can probe with MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES.  Otherwise - we can
> discuss how service support should be discoverable to userspace.
> 
> Memory hotplug is the only source of private memory right now.
> 
> All System RAM on a node shares one configuration: hotplug with a
> different one fails with -EBUSY.
> 
> Costs and known limits
> ======================
> 
>   - ZONELIST_PRIVATE is a third zonelist per pgdat; with NODES_SHIFT=10
>     that is about 80KB per possible node, though a private zonelist
>     holds at most one node's zones.
> 
>     local-only zonelists can be space-optimized if this matters.
> 
>   - Free page reporting reports free private pages like any others.
> 
>   - Tasks are OOM-scored by all of their resident memory,
>     private pages included.
> 
> Changes since v5 ("Private Memory NUMA Nodes")
> ==============================================
> 
>   - Reordered so the N_MEMORY audit (patches 1-26) comes first and can
>     be reviewed (and merged) on its own if desired.
>   - Capabilities became memory features with node states, so a service
>     can be written in terms of itself: reclaim walks N_MEMORY_RECLAIM,
>     compaction N_MEMORY_COMPACTION.
>   - The capability set is pared down to COMPACTION, RECLAIM and
>     MEMPOLICY for the first run.  DEMOTION, NUMA_BALANCING, and
>     compressed RAM support are deferred.
>   - The private zonelist is now local-only. A fallback variant can be
>     added if a use case needs one.
>   - cpuset and OOM semantics are worked out:
>       - cpuset.mems governs private nodes
>       - private-only request inherits the parent's common nodes.
>   - Private bindings are an explicit uapi flag, MPOL_F_PRIVATE_NODES,
>     rather than inferred from the nodemask.
>   - Exhausting private placement fails the fault with SIGBUS, as an
>     exhausted HugeTLB pool does, instead of invoking the OOM killer.
>     OOM support can be added later, but this keeps initial support
>     reasonable simple.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
> ---

> On 2026-11-22 11:51 -0500, Yury Norov wrote:
> > On Fri, Nov 20, 2026 at 01:08:51PM -0500, Gregory Price via B4 Relay wrote:
> > > This is v6 of the Private NUMA node series. The series falls into four

> > 
> 
> I don't see how this would reduce the patch count substatially, you
> still need to convert existing N_MEMORY users and need to differentiate
> between general purpose memory nodes and private memory nodes.

Please check this quick attempt with my codex. The patch count is reduced
to 52:

https://github.com/norov/linux/tree/private-nodes-v6-n-memory-folded

The brief summary for dropped/simplified patches is:

02    ->   dropped - State helpers: no publication/clearing helpers needed.
06\u201311 ->   dropped - Migration, tiers, DAMON, scheduler, stack locality:
           existing N_MEMORY checks already select ordinary memory.
14\u201315 ->   dropped - Hash distribution, kswapd recovery: existing N_MEMORY
           counts remain correct.
03 -> 02 - Common-memory state: documentation only; no new state or sysfs
           attribute.
05 -> 04 - Interleave/tmpfs policies: only the three-line weighted-interleave
           hotplug filter remains.
12 -> 05 - Reclaim: only hotplug kswapd gating remains; iterator conversion
           moves to the reclaim-state patch.
13 -> 06 - Compaction: only system-wide/proactive filtering and hotplug
           kcompactd gating remain.
16 -> 07 - OOM constraints: only capacity-summing intersections remain.
27 -> 18 - Private-memory state: expands to 16 files; topology/accounting
           users must include both memory sets.
31 -> 22 - Cpuset handling: requires ordinary memory while preserving
           allowed private nodes in the returned mask.
44 -> 36,
46 -> 38,
50 -> 42 - Service states: direct updates at boot,
           online, and offline sites replace shared helpers, increasing
           duplication.

The new N_MEMORY_NOALLOC patch is not split intentionally. If you do it, it
would probably turn into 4 individual patches.

The more important thing is that N_MEMORY and the proposed N_MEMORY_NOALLOC
is a disjoint, contrary to N_MEMORY and N_MEMORY_COMMON.
 
> And N_MEMORY_NOALLOC is not a good name.

Sure, I'm not attached to any particular name. Although,
N_MEMORY_COMMON nothing better to me. It answers the question
'what for this thing' even worse.

Thanks,
Yury

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3 00/12] nfsd: various delegated timestamp fixes

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 01/12] nfsd: don't hold inode_lock while waiting for a delegation in nfsd_setattr()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFS server where it waits for a delegation to be returned while holding the inode lock, causing the SETATTR operation to fail with NFS4ERR_DELAY. The patch drops the inode lock during the wait and restarts the SETATTR operation if necessary. It also ensures that the file system's attributes are updated atomically with the attempt to change the inode.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 02/12] nfsd: take freeze protection before updating delegation timestamps
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a bug in the NFS server where it can modify a frozen filesystem by updating delegation timestamps without holding freeze protection. The patch takes freeze protection before updating delegation timestamps in three functions: cb_getattr_update_times(), nfsd_update_cmtime_attr(), and nfsd4_finalize_deleg_timestamps(). It also introduces pinning of fi_deleg_file to prevent racing DELEGRETURN or revocation from putting the file open. This ensures that the filesystem remains frozen even when updating delegation timestamps, preventing potential data corruption.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 03/12] nfsd: count a delegation in cl_delegs_in_recall only once
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFS server where a delegation is counted multiple times when recalled, leading to incorrect client status and preventing courtesy clients from being re-established. The fix involves checking if the recall has already been processed before incrementing the count of delegations in recall, ensuring that nfsd_change_deleg_cb() decrements the count only once at F_UNLCK. This prevents a leaked count that keeps nfs4_anylock_blockers() true and blocks clients from becoming courtesy clients again.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 04/12] nfsd: don't grant write delegations to NFSv4.0 clients on CLAIM_PREVIOUS
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents NFSv4.0 clients from receiving write delegations when reclaiming a file during the grace period, which can cause issues with GETATTR operations. The patch adds a check to the nfs4_open_delegation function for CLAIM_PREVIOUS claims, ensuring that only read-only delegations are granted in this scenario. This fix addresses a problem introduced by enabling write delegation support and is based on a review of existing code comments.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 05/12] nfsd: set ctime when a SETATTR with delegated times changes other attributes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where the ctime of a file was not being updated when a SETATTR request with delegated times changed other attributes. The patch adds ATTR_CTIME to the iattr structure unless the request is a delegated atime-only update, ensuring that ctime is updated whenever any attribute changes occur. Additionally, if a delegated mtime fails vetting, ctime will be moved to the current time instead of leaving it unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 06/12] nfsd: pin the client while a GETATTR holds a conflicting delegation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug where a client could be destroyed while waiting for a GETATTR reply, causing the server to access a freed client. To prevent this, it introduces two new functions: nfsd4_get_leased_deleg and nfsd4_put_leased_deleg. These functions take a reference on both the delegation and the client while holding the flc_lock, ensuring that the client remains alive until the lease is released. This approach addresses the issue of conflicting delegations during GETATTR operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 07/12] nfsd: recall when a CB_GETATTR reply omits the size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue in the NFSv4 callback code where a CB_GETATTR reply without the SIZE attribute would cause the file size to be reported incorrectly, leading to incorrect delegation recalls. The patch adds a new field ncf_cb_bitmap0 to hold word 0 of the reply's bitmap and checks for this condition in nfsd4_cb_getattr_done(). If the SIZE attribute is missing, the callback is failed and the delegation is recalled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 08/12] nfsd: apply delegated times in a separate times-only setattr
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the handling of delegated times in NFSv4. It separates the application of delegated times into a separate 'times-only' setattr call, which avoids issues with ownership checks and attribute reporting. The patch also adds new fields to store delegated atime and mtime values, and updates various functions to handle these changes. Additionally, it removes the ATTR_DELEG branch from __nfsd_setattr() and always adds ATTR_CTIME. This change improves the handling of delegated times in NFSv4 and fixes several issues related to attribute reporting and ownership checks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 09/12] nfsd: grant a plain read delegation when timestamps are wanted on a read open
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFS server's delegation handling to grant a plain read delegation when a client requests delegated timestamps on a read open operation. This is done by declining the attribute delegation request, as per RFC 9754 section 5, and instead granting a standard read delegation. The patch addresses an issue where delegating atime correctly would require exclusive authority over it or merging the times of multiple read holders, which NFSD does not support.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 10/12] nfsd: check fi_had_conflict under deleg_lock before hashing a delegation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the NFSv4 delegation handling code by checking for conflicts under the deleg_lock before hashing a delegation. This prevents a situation where a lease break can occur between setting fi_had_conflict and hashing the delegation, leading to a delegation being granted that is already recalled but not on the del_recall_lru list. The patch addresses an issue introduced by a previous change that removed the need for taking fi_lock in nfsd_break_deleg_cb().

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 11/12] nfsd: take the write delegation grant stat before hashing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFSv4 delegation grant process to take a stat of the file before hashing the delegation. This is done by moving the nfs4_delegation_stat function above nfs4_set_delegation and taking the stat just before hashing. The patch also adds an additional stat after hashing to check for changes in the file's attributes. If either stat fails, the delegation grant is declined. This change addresses a potential issue where a client could receive a stale delegation due to a window of time between hashing and the stat being taken.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 12/12] nfsd: move ctime when CB_GETATTR applies a delegated mtime
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a timestamp update issue in the NFS daemon by always setting the ctime attribute when an applied mtime is set, and only setting the ctime_set flag if the vetted ctime passes validation. This ensures that rejected ctimes are updated to the current time, matching the behavior of SETATTR with delegated times.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes various bugs in the NFSv4 delegated timestamp support, including issues with freeze protection, SETATTR, and CB_GETATTR operations. The patches address problems such as incorrect handling of delegation timestamps, missing ctime updates, and conflicts between GETATTR and delegations. The changes also improve the overall consistency and correctness of the delegated timestamp logic.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the SETATTR operation in nfsd_setattr() waits for a delegation return while still holding inode_lock, which can cause a deadlock when the holder sends WRITEs that flush its dirty data before DELEGRETURN. The author agreed to drop inode_lock across the wait and restructure the code in v2.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern that the code does not hold freeze protection for the export's filesystem when updating delegation timestamps in certain situations, such as CB_GETATTR and DELEGRETURN. The author explained that the issue is due to the fact that freeze protection is taken outside inode_lock, but the update of delegation timestamps can still occur while the filesystem is frozen. To fix this, the author added a check for freeze protection in cb_getattr_update_times() and nfsd4_finalize_deleg_timestamps(), and also modified nfsd4_finalize_deleg_timestamps() to wait for a thaw if necessary.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about NFSv4.0 clients being able to get write delegations during grace, which can lead to incomplete GETATTR requests. The author agrees that the same check as in nfs4_open_delegation() should be applied to CLAIM_PREVIOUS and will add this fix.
review_comments.raw_body:
nfs4_open_delegation() refuses delegations for NFSv4.0 write opens on
CLAIM_NULL and CLAIM_FH, as its comment explains, but CLAIM_PREVIOUS
skips the check. An NFSv4.0 client reclaiming a write open during grace
can therefore get a write delegation, and NFSD can never complete a
GETATTR that the client sends before DELEGRETURN in the same compound.

Apply the same check to CLAIM_PREVIOUS.

Fixes: 1d3dd1d56ce8 ("NFSD: Enable write delegation support")
Reviewed-by: Aurlien Couderc <aurelien.couderc2002@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
---
 fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c | 3 +++
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)

diff --git a/fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c b/fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c
index c2c082006d81..f865548c297b 100644
--- a/fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c
+++ b/fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c
@@ -7542,6 +7542,9 @@ nfs4_open_delegation(struct svc_rqst *rqstp, struct nfsd4_open *open,
 	open->op_recall = false;
 	switch (open->op_claim_type) {
 		case NFS4_OPEN_CLAIM_PREVIOUS:
+			if (open->op_share_access & NFS4_SHARE_ACCESS_WRITE &&
+			    clp->cl_minorversion == 0)
+				goto out_no_deleg;
 			if (!cb_up)
 				open->op_recall = true;
 			break;

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about nfsd_break_deleg_cb() running multiple times per lease, causing cl_delegs_in_recall to be incremented unnecessarily and preventing the client from becoming a courtesy client. The author provided a fix by adding a check for dl_recalled before incrementing the count and setting fi_had_conflict.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about CB_GETATTR replies without SIZE attribute, which caused the waiter to mark the file modified and report an incorrect size. The author added a new bitmap word (ncf_cb_bitmap0) to hold the first word of the reply's bitmap, cleared when the callback is issued. In nfsd4_cb_getattr_done(), a reply without SIZE is now treated as failed, causing the waiter to recall the delegation.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about delegated timestamp handling in SETATTR operations. They acknowledged that the current implementation has issues with EPERM errors for non-owners, incorrect application of ATTR_DELEG, and incomplete reporting of attributes when times are rejected. The author proposed a new approach to decode time_deleg_access and time_deleg_modify into separate fields, apply vetted times with notify_change(ATTR_FORCE), and skip nfsd_setattr() for times-only requests. They also addressed issues with delegated times in CREATE and OPEN operations.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the ctime should be updated when any attribute is changed in a delegated atime update, not just mtime. They added a check to set ATTR_CTIME unless the request is a delegated atime-only update and modified the code to move ctime to the current time if vetting of the delegated mtime fails.
review_comments.raw_body:
__nfsd_setattr() adds ATTR_CTIME only when ATTR_DELEG is clear, to keep
a delegated atime-only update from moving ctime. But ATTR_DELEG is set
for the whole iattr, so a holder's chmod or chown sent along with a
delegated atime changes the mode or owner without updating ctime.

Add ATTR_CTIME unless the request is a delegated atime-only update. A
delegated mtime whose ctime fails vetting now moves ctime to the current
time instead of leaving ctime alone. Since ctime moves, set dl_setattr
whenever the delegated mtime is applied. Otherwise DELEGRETURN of a
written file restamps the vetted mtime and atime to the current time.

Fixes: f9a348e0de19 ("nfsd: don't set the ctime on delegated atime updates")
Signed-off-by: Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

 fs/nfsd/nfs4proc.c | 6 +++---
 fs/nfsd/vfs.c      | 8 +++++---
 2 files changed, 8 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)

diff --git a/fs/nfsd/nfs4proc.c b/fs/nfsd/nfs4proc.c
index b76320c265e1..f8473d0923b8 100644
--- a/fs/nfsd/nfs4proc.c
+++ b/fs/nfsd/nfs4proc.c
@@ -1378,10 +1378,10 @@ vet_deleg_attrs(struct nfsd4_setattr *setattr, struct nfs4_delegation *dp)
 
 	if (setattr->sa_bmval[2] & FATTR4_WORD2_TIME_DELEG_MODIFY) {
 		if (nfsd4_vet_deleg_time(&iattr->ia_mtime, &dp->dl_mtime, &now)) {
+			/* ctime moves too, so DELEGRETURN needn't restamp */
+			dp->dl_setattr = true;
 			iattr->ia_ctime = iattr->ia_mtime;
-			if (nfsd4_vet_deleg_time(&iattr->ia_ctime, &dp->dl_ctime, &now))
-				dp->dl_setattr = true;
-			else
+			if (!nfsd4_vet_deleg_time(&iattr->ia_ctime, &dp->dl_ctime, &now))
 				iattr->ia_valid &= ~(ATTR_CTIME | ATTR_CTIME_SET);
 		} else {
 			iattr->ia_valid &= ~(ATTR_CTIME | ATTR_CTIME_SET |
diff --git a/fs/nfsd/vfs.c b/fs/nfsd/vfs.c
index 4a5674e583cc..7bc251d55c3c 100644
--- a/fs/nfsd/vfs.c
+++ b/fs/nfsd/vfs.c
@@ -513,10 +513,12 @@ static int __nfsd_setattr(struct dentry *dentry, struct iattr *iap)
 	/*
 	 * If ATTR_DELEG is set, then this is an update from a client that
 	 * holds a delegation. If this is an update for only the atime, the
-	 * ctime should not be changed. If the update contains the mtime
-	 * too, then ATTR_CTIME should already be set.
+	 * ctime should not be changed. Any other attribute change, such as
+	 * a mode or owner change sent along with a delegated atime, must
+	 * update the ctime.
 	 */
-	if (!(iap->ia_valid & ATTR_DELEG))
+	if (!(iap->ia_valid & ATTR_DELEG) ||
+	    (iap->ia_valid & ~(ATTR_DELEG | ATTR_ATIME | ATTR_ATIME_SET)))
 		iap->ia_valid |= ATTR_CTIME;
 
 	return notify_change(&nop_mnt_idmap, dentry, iap, NULL);

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] firmware: arm_sdei_nmi: Send the backtrace IPI to CPUs with SDEI masked

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a lockup issue on idle CPUs caused by SDEI NMI backtraces. The problem occurs when an event is signaled to all CPUs, including those in a power-down state where SDEI is masked. To fix this, the patches prevent event 0 from being sent to masked PEs and send regular backtrace IPIs to these CPUs instead. This approach ensures that the system remains responsive even during idle states.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern that the patch does not address the issue of TF-A refusing to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks right after the check still takes the SGI. The author explains that this is due to the handshake change since the earlier version and asks Jinjie to run the new version on HIP12.
review_comments.raw_body:
The SDEI NMI backtrace signals event 0 to every other CPU, including the
ones in a power-down idle state, where the kernel has SDEI masked. TF-A
acknowledges the SGI behind event 0 on a masked PE and never ends it,
and the PE takes no Non-secure interrupt again. Jinjie hit it on a
384-CPU HIP12, where one sysrq-l locked up the machine.

Patch 1 keeps event 0 away from masked PEs. Patch 2 sends the regular
backtrace IPI to the CPUs that SDEI refused, which wakes them.

TF-A v2.13 and later refuse to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks
right after the check still takes the SGI. The TF-A fix is under review:

  https://review.trustedfirmware.org/c/TF-A/trusted-firmware-a/+/55414

Tested under QEMU TCG with TF-A built without that check, 4 CPUs. One
CPU masks and unmasks SDEI in a loop, through cpu_pm, the mask calls and
CPU hotplug, while another signals it; sysrq-l afterwards. Signalling
with plain SMCs, as the kernel does now, wedges the target. With the
series every run passed, lockdep included, and a panic in the middle of
it completes.

Jinjie ran an earlier version on HIP12 with the power-down state
enabled: sysrq-l got 384/384 answers every run. The handshake has
changed since; Jinjie, could you give this one a run as well?

version_history.subject: [PATCH] drm/i915/gem: Skip writeback of shmem folios with extra references

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the drm/i915/gem module to skip writeback of shmem folios that have extra references, preventing a race condition where a stale TLB entry can still store data to an unmapped folio until the TLB is flushed. The change ensures that such folios are left to reclaim as mapped ones would be, rather than being written back from swap without the stored data.

review_comments.author: Andi Shyti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Andi Shyti noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio has extra references beyond the page cache and writeback_iter(), which can lead to stale TLB entries allowing writes through, and requested checking for this condition in addition to the existing folio_mapped() check.

Reviewer Andi Shyti pointed out that the patch is unnecessary because the i915 writeback iterator already skips shmem folios in the described case, making the new refcount check redundant.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Kiryl,

On Thu, Nov 19, 2026 at 01:42:41PM +0000, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) wrote:

---

I don't think we need this fix in the current tree. The i915
writeback iterator already skips the shmem folio in the case you
describe, so the new refcount check doesn't change the outcome.

Thanks,
Andi

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: Author realized that __shmem_writeback() never runs for shmem folios due to PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY not being set, and questions the purpose of writeback in this context.
review_comments.raw_body:
Oh. It took me a while to see why.

__shmem_writeback() asks writeback_iter() for PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY
folios, and shmem never sets that tag, its ->dirty_folio is
noop_dirty_folio(). So the loop body never runs for any folio, and
hasn't since 776a853a43c9 ("i915: Use writeback_iter()").

That makes me question the whole writeback thing. What's going on
there, and what's the plan?

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Christoph Hellwig expressed strong disagreement with the patch, stating that it's an indication of a deeper issue in drm code managing tmpfs and suggested removing the problematic code path altogether.
review_comments.raw_body:
I (and others) have been asking forever to get drm out of micro-managing
tmpfs.  I guess given that this code path hasn't worked for a year and
a half is a pretty good indicator that this instance should simply
go away.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] arm64: sdei: add sdei_nmi.disabled= to keep the GIC NMI path reachable
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch to add sdei_nmi.disabled= option to keep GIC NMI path reachable, with suggested simplifications and improvements.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)
review_comments.summary: Raised a technical concern about the patch's logic and suggested simplifications to avoid unnecessary code.

review_comments.author: Jinjie Ruan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged Kiryl's suggestion and agreed to update the code, showing willingness to address concerns.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Kiryl,

\u5728 2026/11/25 2:12, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) \u5199\u9053:
> On Mon, Nov 23, 2026 at 11:32:22AM +0800, Jinjie Ruan wrote:
>> While the SDEI cross-CPU NMI is active it claims every cross-CPU
>> backtrace, so on a platform whose firmware exposes SDEI event 0
>> the irqchip NMI path can never be used.  There is no way to opt out.
>>
>> Add a boot parameter "sdei_nmi.disabled".
>>
>> With sdei_nmi.disabled=1, the SDEI NMI stays registered and simply
>> declines every request, so arch_trigger_cpumask_backtrace() falls
>> through to its IPI path and smp_send_stop() skips its SDEI rung.
> 
> Why keep event 0 registered and enabled when the switch is on?

These original codes are left for testing the IPI as NMI function.

> 
> If sdei_nmi_init() returns before sdei_event_register(),
> sdei_nmi_available stays false and both hooks already decline.

You are absolutely correct. sdei_nmi_available itself can block all SDEI
operations, which can simplify many things.

> 
> Then the flag is read only at init and can be __initdata. None of the
> other hunks are needed. The check in sdei_nmi_stop_cpus() is not
> reachable anyway: smp_send_stop() calls it only after sdei_nmi_active().

Yes, you are right! I will update them.

Best regards,
Jinjie

> 
> --
>   Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov
